column2: This Final Environmental Statement covers Operation BREAKTHROUGH, a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development research and development program to speed up factory-built (industrialized) housing by demonstrating 22 innovative housing systems on nine prototype sites in eight areas of the country, including Jersey City, Kalamazoo, Macon, Memphis, St. Louis, Sacramento, Indianapolis, Seattle, and King County, Washington. The sites range from downtown urban renewal parcels to suburban parcels and are intended to house a mix of income levels and racial groups. HUD considered four alternatives — doing nothing, pursuing technology alone without addressing market and regulatory barriers, using a different number or character of demonstration sites (such as a single 'housing fair' or federal-land-only sites), and limiting each site to one housing system — and rejected all four in favor of the current design. Expected environmental effects include increased stormwater runoff from paving, visual changes, added load on local schools and sewers, construction erosion, and, at Jersey City specifically, air-quality and fuel-use effects from an on-site 'total energy' power plant that reuses waste heat; HUD says site-by-site measures (stormwater holding basins at Indianapolis, leaching catch basins at Kalamazoo, a lake-turnover siphon at Macon, and a noise berm at Memphis) address these effects. Nine federal agencies commented; the main criticisms were that the statement lacked site-by-site detail required under Section 102(2)(C) of NEPA, that erosion controls and non-wood materials needed more discussion, and that total energy systems are not new and not necessarily more efficient than conventional electric service on an annual basis.

column2: Operation BREAKTHROUGH is a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development research and development program, announced in 1969 by Secretary George Romney, to speed up volume production of industrialized (factory-built) housing. Under it, HUD selected 22 housing systems and is demonstrating them on nine prototype sites in eight areas — Indianapolis, Jersey City, Kalamazoo, Macon, Memphis, Sacramento, St. Louis, Seattle, and King County, Washington — combining new building materials and methods with cluster site planning, with construction running from late 1970 through projected completion in 1972–1973. The Jersey City site additionally tests a 'total energy' plant (an on-site power plant that generates electricity and reuses waste heat for hot water, heating, and cooling) and a Swedish-developed pneumatic trash collection system that pulls refuse through sealed vacuum tubing directly from disposal chutes to a central compacting location.

column2: The nine prototype sites span central-city urban renewal parcels and suburban neighborhoods and are designed to house a mix of income levels and racial groups, including subsidized units, cooperatives, student housing, and public housing. Specific locations include a 6.35-acre downtown Jersey City block at Newark Avenue and John F. Kennedy Boulevard, one block from the central business district; a 15.9-acre parcel in the Court Avenue Urban Renewal Area in downtown Memphis between the CBD and the University of Tennessee Medical Center; two neighboring parcels totaling 15.5 acres in the Mill Creek Urban Renewal Area in downtown St. Louis near St. Louis University; a plateau in Kalamazoo overlooking a city park, a lake, and an adjacent municipal water-supply well field; and a suburban site in King County. Local school capacity was a concern at Jersey City, where a supplemental school will be built and leased to the Jersey City school department.

column2: HUD considered and rejected four alternatives to the proposed program. First, doing nothing was dismissed as unrealistic given the scale of the national housing shortage. Second, a technology-only program that ignored regulatory and market barriers was rejected because the resulting technology would not be widely adopted. Third, a different number or character of demonstration sites — for example, a single 'housing fair' with one of each system, or sites only on federal land — was rejected in favor of a national competition selecting sites that would demonstrate both housing and community development in varied settings. Fourth, a site-design philosophy limiting each site to a single housing system was rejected so that more of the competitively selected systems could be demonstrated within budget. In addition, for the Jersey City site, the statement considers conventional grid electricity plus separate on-site heating and cooling as the alternative to the total energy plant, and discusses fuel cells (then experimental, with a prototype installation in a single-family home in Farmington, Connecticut) as a longer-term option that HUD says is not yet ready.

column2: Anticipated adverse effects include changes in storm runoff from paving open land, visual impacts of changing land use to housing, added burden on local schools and sewers, and possible effects on adjacent property values; HUD says each has been addressed in design. Site-specific water measures include earthmoving to create stormwater holding basins at Indianapolis, leaching catch basins at Kalamazoo that filter first-flush runoff through permeable soil before it reaches the lake and municipal well field, and a siphon system at Macon to turn over lake water and prevent eutrophication (nutrient buildup that depletes oxygen). At Memphis, measurements found the site did not comply with HUD Circular 1390.2 on noise, so an earth berm was built to shield it; that circular sets binding limits — sites exceeding 80 dB(A) for 60 minutes per 24 hours are 'unacceptable,' and interior sleeping quarters must generally stay below 55 dB(A). At Jersey City, the total energy plant is projected to use a little more than half the fuel that separate on-site heating/cooling plus grid electricity would require, with lower thermal and air pollution. Roughly two-thirds of the 22 selected housing systems use concrete, metal, or plastic rather than wood, which HUD says will ease pressure on U.S. timber supplies.

column2: Written comments came from nine federal bodies: the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, the Department of Agriculture, the Army Corps of Engineers, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Commerce, the Federal Power Commission, and several HUD offices. EPA said site-specific air pollution effects could not be evaluated without a separate impact statement for each of the eight areas, and asked for more detail on construction-phase erosion controls, non-wood materials, water supply and wastewater handling, and HUD's Interim Noise Standards. Interior called the statement a good program description but said it lacked the detail required under Section 102(2)(C) of NEPA, and raised concerns about social effects of dense multistory housing, conflicts with mineral-resource lands, and use of solid-waste materials in construction. Agriculture warned that building on poor-quality land (flood-prone, high shrink-swell, or erosion-prone soils) has produced distressed communities in the past. HEW asked how the technology would help renovate existing substandard urban units and noted the statement omitted resident training in home use and maintenance. The Army Corps asked how mass-produced housing would fit with existing neighborhoods. The Federal Power Commission observed that total energy systems are not new (507 were listed in a 1971 directory, though fewer than 10% serve residences) and are not necessarily more efficient than conventional electrical systems on an annual basis, and suggested attention to fuel cells; HUD's Assistant Secretary Harold B. Finger replied that residential operating data is scarce (one-third of existing residential total energy plants are in Johnson County, Kansas, stemming from one developer's dispute with the local utility), which is why the Jersey City demonstration is needed.
